hooks.text: The Moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist.
A glowing white moon rock shattered our lunar history.
Why did a single bright moon rock shatter lunar science?

title: The Moon Rock That Broke Lunar History
description: Apollo 16 returned with bright lunar rocks that challenged everything we thought we knew about the Moon's ancient magma ocean.

beats.text: The Moon's brightest rocks are too young to exist.
beats.visual: Apollo photograph of the bright lunar highlands on the far side of the Moon, 1972

beats.text: In 1972, Apollo 16 astronauts returned stunningly bright stones called anorthosite from the lunar highlands.
beats.visual: Apollo 16 astronaut John Young collecting lunar rock samples on the Moon, 1972

beats.text: For decades, experts believed these rocks floated like icebergs atop a primordial magma ocean.
beats.visual: Artist's illustration of the early Moon covered in a glowing global magma ocean

beats.text: This coarse-grained crust is 90 percent plagioclase feldspar, a mineral that is less dense than liquid magma.
beats.visual: Macrophotograph of anorthosite rock showing large plagioclase feldspar crystals

beats.text: But in 2011, researchers used precise chemical dating on lunar Sample 60025 and found it was only 4.36 billion years old.
beats.visual: Cleanroom photograph of lunar Sample 60025 in a sterile NASA lab

beats.text: This age is over 100 million years too young for a crust formed at the Moon's birth.
beats.visual: Artist's illustration of a giant asteroid impact bombarding the early Moon

beats.text: This discovery suggests the Moon was volcanically active much later than scientists ever imagined.
beats.visual: Artist's illustration of active volcanic eruptions on the ancient lunar surface

beats.text: Geologists are now forced to rewrite the entire ancient history of our closest neighbor.
beats.visual: Telescopic photograph of the full Moon showing the reflective highlands

better_than_last: Increased word count to 121 and specifically addressed the reviewer's point about late volcanic activity to strengthen the twist and loop.
